title: Checkpoint: Number, Place, and the Person Concerned
summary: A cumulative examination of sections eight to ten: the plural in three cases with the numerals that govern them, the locative against the accusative of direction, and the dative with the constructions built on it.

drills.stem: What is the nominative plural of **katė**?
drills.explanation: Feminine -ė makes -ės. *kates* is the accusative plural and *kačių* the genitive plural, in which the t softens to č.
*mėgti* governs the accusative (¶39), and the accusative plural of a -ė noun is -es. *katės* is the nominative and could only be a subject.
The adjective agrees in gender and number, and *du* takes the nominative plural. *dešimt* governs the genitive plural, so the last should be *dešimt knygų*.

drills.stem: *Berniukas dirba* becomes *Berniukai dirba* in the plural. What does this show about the verb?
options: That the verb agrees with the subject in number.
That one form serves the whole third person, singular and plural alike.
That the plural subject requires the first-person ending.
drills.explanation: The third person is indifferent to number in every Lithuanian verb (¶57). Only the first and second persons have separate plural endings.

drills.stem: **Vaikas turi vieną gerą knygą.** How many words change form if *vieną* becomes *dešimt*?
drills.explanation: Three besides nothing else: *vieną* → *dešimt*, and *gerą knygą* → *gerų knygų*, the genitive plural that *dešimt* governs, the adjective following its noun. *vaikas* and *turi* are untouched — the numeral overrides the case the verb would have required, but it does not touch the subject.

drills.stem: Complete: **Ji dirba ____.** (She works at the university.)
drills.explanation: The locative needs no preposition; the ending -e carries "at" entire. *į universitetą* would say she is travelling there.

drills.stem: You are in Vilnius and mean to reach Kaunas. Which is right?
drills.explanation: *eiti* is to go on foot and *važiuoti* by vehicle — a distinction English does not draw and Lithuanian insists on. The locative *Kaune* would say you are already there.

drills.stem: Which of these state where something **is**, rather than where it is going?
drills.explanation: A genitive after *ant*, a locative plural, and an instrumental after *po* all state position. Only *į* with the accusative expresses motion towards.

drills.stem: Which adverb answers *kur?* without any noun or preposition at all?
drills.explanation: *namie*, at home — a place adverb standing outside the noun paradigm entirely (*name* would mean "in the building"). *dažnai*, *retai* and *kartais* answer how often, not where.

drills.stem: **Aš esu naujoje kavinėje.** How many words change form if you are going *into* the new café instead?
drills.explanation: Two: *naujoje kavinėje* → *naują kavinę*, the adjective following its noun out of the locative into the accusative that *į* governs. The verb is replaced rather than reshaped, and the preposition is added rather than changed.

drills.stem: What is the dative singular of **brolis**?
drills.explanation: Masculine -is makes -iui. *brolio* is the genitive, *brolyje* the locative, *brolį* the accusative — four cases, four endings, all built on the same stem.
*reikia* is impersonal and has no subject: the needer stands in the dative *jai* and what is needed in the genitive *pinigų*. Supplying an accusative is the error English invites.
*padėti* governs the dative, so *mamą* is wrong. *patikti* and *skambinti* likewise take the dative — a group of common verbs where English supplies a direct object and Lithuanian does not.

drills.stem: **Man patinka knygos.** Which word is the grammatical subject?
drills.explanation: The thing liked is the subject and stands in the nominative; the liker is put in the dative. That is why the verb would change with the number of books and never with the number of people (¶68).

drills.stem: **Aš mėgstu naują knygą.** Rewritten with *patikti* so as to mean the same, how many words of the new sentence differ in form from the old?
drills.explanation: The sentence becomes *Man patinka nauja knyga*: *aš* → *man*, *mėgstu* → *patinka*, and *naują knygą* → *nauja knyga*, the object becoming the subject and giving up its accusative, adjective and all. Every one of the four words is altered.

drills.stem: Complete: **Aš duodu knygą ____.** (I give the book to my brother.)
drills.explanation: A verb of giving has two objects: the thing in the accusative and the person in the dative (¶66). *brolį* would leave the sentence with two accusatives and nothing to say who received the book.

drills.stem: Which of these are correctly formed **locatives**?
drills.explanation: -oje, -ėje and -uje are the three commonest locative endings. *stalo* is the genitive of *stalas*, as after *ant*; its locative would be *stale*.

drills.title: Savaitgalis
drills.passage: Eglė gyvena Kaune, o jos brolis Tomas — Vilniuje. Savaitgalį Eglė važiuoja į Vilnių. Tomas laukia jos stotyje. Eglė veža jam dovaną: dvi knygas ir puodelį. Tomui patinka knygos, bet jam nereikia puodelio — jis turi dešimt puodelių. Vakare jie eina į kavinę. Kavinė yra prie stoties. Eglei patinka Vilnius, bet ji nemėgsta didelių miestų.
drills.translation: Eglė lives in Kaunas, and her brother Tomas in Vilnius. At the weekend Eglė travels to Vilnius. Tomas waits for her at the station. Eglė brings him a present: two books and a cup. Tomas likes books, but he does not need the cup — he has ten cups. In the evening they go to a café. The café is near the station. Eglė likes Vilnius, but she does not like big cities.

questions.explanation: *Tomui patinka knygos.* The cup is precisely what he does not need, having ten already. The dative *Tomui* names the person who likes, and *knygos* is the subject (¶68).

questions.stem: Which of these does the passage support?
questions.explanation: She does *not* like big cities — *nemėgsta didelių miestų*, where the negation puts the object into the genitive plural (¶31, ¶55), though she likes Vilnius itself.

questions.stem: The passage has **Eglė veža jam dvi knygas.** How many words change form if she brings him *ten* books instead of two?
questions.explanation: Two: *dvi* → *dešimt*, and *knygas* → *knygų*, since *dešimt* governs the genitive plural where *dvi* left the case to the verb (¶58). *Eglė*, *veža* and the dative *jam* are all untouched.
